question: A queued node fails while nobody is watching — does the dispatcher stop, or skip that node and keep draining?

options.label: Stop draining entirely and wait for a human
options.reason: It is what ADR 0017 already decided for one drain — "a queued chain stops at the first rejection or failure", so that four more nodes are never built on top of a result a human turned down. A dispatcher that loops forever would quietly convert that rule into "stops until the next cycle", which is not stopping at all. Halting also makes the failure impossible to miss: the queue stops moving, which is the loudest signal an unattended process has.
options.costLater: One unrelated failure — a flaky setup command, a network blip in `dispatch.setup` — idles the whole queue until somebody returns, which is the cost the dispatcher existed to remove. It also needs a resume that is not just a restart, or the user's fix is "turn it off and on again".

options.label: Skip the failed node and its dependents, keep draining the rest
options.reason: The rule ADR 0017 protects is about a chain: nothing is built on a result a human has not seen. A node in a different part of the graph is not on that chain and is not endangered by this failure. Skipping the subtree and continuing keeps the unattended run productive through a flake instead of parking it.
options.costLater: It has to compute the dependent subtree correctly every time, and a mistake there is exactly the failure ADR 0017 forbids — work built on a rejected result, produced unattended, found later. The user also returns to a mixed pile: some finished, some skipped, some failed, and has to reconstruct what happened from logs rather than from where the queue stopped.

options.label: Keep going, but stop the whole dispatcher after N failures in a cycle
options.reason: It separates a flake from a fault: one failure is noise and the queue rides through it, several in a row means something is broken about this machine or this base and no further spending is justified. The threshold is one number in .sober/config.jsonc, beside `concurrency` and `timeoutMinutes` which are already exactly this kind of governor.
options.costLater: N is a number nobody can pick correctly, and the wrong value fails in both directions — too low and it is stop-and-wait with extra machinery, too high and it burns a chain of runs on a broken base before noticing. It is also the only option here that still spends money after the first failure, so its worst case costs the most.
